title: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), columns I-V
source: Israel Museum photograph of scroll 1QpHab (Digital Dead Sea Scrolls) + ETCBC dss transcription (Abegg; CC BY-NC 4.0) + English of W. H. Brownlee, BASOR 112 (1948), public domain
description: The first five columns of the Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran Cave 1, a line-by-line explanation of Habakkuk 1 that names the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest and the Kittim, each column shown on the photograph of the scroll.
introduction:
The Habakkuk Commentary (Pesher Habakkuk, 1QpHab) is one of the seven scrolls found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. It quotes the first two chapters of the book of Habakkuk a phrase at a time and explains each quotation with the word pesher ("its meaning"), applying the prophet's words to the community's own time: the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest, the Man of the Lie, and the Kittim, a foreign power usually identified with Rome. The scroll is about 1.48 m long and is kept in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem (inv. 95.57/28). On the evidence of its handwriting it is usually dated to the late first century BCE.

This entry gives columns I to V of the 13 surviving columns (Habakkuk 1:1-16); columns VI to XIII (Habakkuk 1:16 to 2:20) follow in the next entry. Each section is one column. The Hebrew is the scroll's own text with its column and line numbers, from the transcription of Martin G. Abegg Jr. and colleagues in the ETCBC "dss" dataset. Square brackets mark letters lost from the leather and restored by the editors; a dot under a letter marks an uncertain reading; ⟨ ⟩ marks letters written above the line; an ellipsis marks lost letters that are not restored.

The English is the complete translation of the scroll by William H. Brownlee, published in December 1948. Brownlee kept the scroll's columns. In his notation a diagonal line (/) marks the start of a new line of the scroll, words in parentheses are his conjectural restorations, a row of dots (shown here as …) is a lacuna, ? marks traces of letters, # marks letters that can be read but not translated, and words between asterisks were moved across a line division. His quotations of Habakkuk are set in italics. Superscript numbers give the lines of the scroll. In columns I and II they stand where each line of the scroll begins in the English, checked against the Hebrew line by line; in columns III to V they are the numbers Brownlee printed in his margin, beside the printed line on which each line of the scroll begins.

The photographs are the Israel Museum's own images of the scroll from its Digital Dead Sea Scrolls site, one image per column. Columns I and II, and the lower lines of every column, are damaged on the scroll itself; column II runs across the crack between the two pieces into which the opening of the scroll is broken.
translator_notes: Brownlee's translation of 1948 predates later work on the scroll; his restorations in parentheses sometimes differ from the restorations in square brackets in the Hebrew transcription.
Footnote numbers in Brownlee's text are omitted. Each printed row of dots is shown as a single ellipsis.

translation.text:
1(At kings) he scoffs;
And princes are laughable to him.

2Its meaning is that / they laugh at the great; they are scornful 3of the esteemed. Of / righteous * kings * are they abusive. They scoff at a numerous people.

4Yea he / doth laugh at each fortress;
He heaps up the earth and takes it.

5(Its) meaning (con)cerns the rulers of the Chittiim, who scorn 6the fortresses of the peoples and with ridicule laugh at them. / With 7a numerous people they surround them to take them; and with terror 8and dread / are they given into their hands who reduce to ruins those 9dwelling / in them.

10Then the wind changes and removes;
Yet this man makes his strength / his god.

11(Its) meaning (con)cerns the rulers of the Chittiim / who, acting upon the advice of the house of “guil(t)” “remove” a man / from 13before his fellows ruli(ng) … ?. After this they proceed / to destroy the peo(ples).

(Yet) this man (makes) his strength his god.

14Its meaning (concerns) … (al)l the peoples 15… ?

translation.text:
1For judgment, hast thou appointed him;
O Rock, for his chastising hast thou ordained him.
2Too pure of eyes art thou / to look upon evil;
And to countenance wrong-doing thou art unable. /

3The meaning of the passage is that God will not destroy His people 4by the hand of the nations; / but by the hand of His elect, God will give the judgment of all the nations; and in their chastisement / 5shall suffer all the wicked from among His people who keep His 6commandments / in the time of their distress; for he of whom it 7speaks is “too pure of eyes to look / upon evil.” The meaning of this 8is that they do not lust after their eyes to the doom / of wickedness.

Why do ye countenance the treacherous and keep silence
9While / the wicked * doth swallow * one more righteous
than himself?

10Its meaning concerns the house of Absalom / and the men of their counsel who were silent at the reproof of the Teacher of 11Righteousness / and did not help him against the Man of the Lie, who 12had rejected / the Law among all peo(ple)s.

Thou hast made man as the fish of the sea, /
13As a crawling thing over which to rule.
He brings (them) all up (with a h)ook
And fishes them out with his net, /
14And gathers them (into his seine;
He sacrifices) to his net;
15Wherefore, he rejoices / (and exul)ts;
(Wherefore, he burns incense to his seine,
For thereby) his ration is (lib)eral, /
16(And his food is abundant!)

(Its meaning concerns) …
